title: Monopoly Round-Up: Did Bernie Sanders Set the Terms for the Midterm Elections?
author: Lee Hepner
content:
There's a lot of good and bad monopoly news this week, as usual. The Federal
Trade Commission is making tentative moves on surveillance pricing, online
food delivery is consolidating, and healthcare middlemen are in the crosshairs
of the Trump Administration. All of that and a lot more is below the jump, for
paid subscribers only.

But we're two days away from what could be a pivotal midterm election, so I
want to spend a bit of time on that. Affordability, corruption, artificial
intelligence, the Iran War and Gaza, healthcare, and billionaires are on the
ballot. Inflation is persistent, the tech stocks keeping the market afloat
just [wiped out](https://www.nbcnews.com/business/markets/tech-stocks-nasdaq-
ai-boom-fears-deepen-rcna606512) $1 trillion in value, and artificial
intelligence is making everything more expensive and less secure. Air is
leaving the AI bubble; perhaps a light breeze moves through your hair.

To understand the stakes, I wanted to start with the Trump victory in 2024,
and how far we've come. With a more
[diverse](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2025/06/26/behind-
trumps-2024-victory-a-more-racially-and-ethnically-diverse-voter-coalition/)
voter base than 2016 or 2020, Trump became the first Republican presidential
candidate in 20 years to have won the [popular
vote](https://www.factcheck.org/2024/11/trump-won-the-popular-vote-contrary-
to-claims-online/), finally having achieved the legitimacy he sought.
Democrats were shattered, [helpless and
discredited](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/why-does-the-biden-white-
house-hate), having lied about Biden's mental acuity dealing with a very
bitter public, angry about the cost of living. His successor, Kamala Harris,
had dithered, unable to even defend Lina Khan after her billionaire donor ally
Reid Hoffman demanded she fire Khan during the campaign. She lost, and it was
humiliating. For a few months, Trump, Elon Musk and DOGE ransacked liberal
pride, getting rid of USAID, proudly slashing government workers, and seizing
control of scientific and academic research funding choices.

But then something interesting happened among Democrats. Bernie Sanders,
considered a left-wing radical, launched what he called the "Fight Oligarchy"
tour.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!KSRq!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd3c07ebf-053c-467f-93c5-be6bb97e7e20_791x696.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!KSRq!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd3c07ebf-053c-467f-93c5-be6bb97e7e20_791x696.png)

I want to revisit a BIG [post](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/monopoly-
round-up-the-populist-revolt) from February 2025 about it, which we called a
"populist revolt." BIG saw it as the political support for what had been,
under Biden, a mostly insider crusade against corporate power.

A year and a half later, has it come to pass? I've gone over a bunch of the
ads and messages in these midterm campaigns, and there are definite signs that
it has, and that we're in a distinctly populist moment in American politics.
Yet the more important question is not just whether surging populism on the
left can win elections, but whether it can produce a governing agenda going
forward. And, as I'll discuss below, that battle is taking place within the
Democratic Party, but it's
[coming](https://www.ft.com/content/a97de5ca-484e-4ed9-84e0-958b90b85ef8?syn-25a6b1a6=1)
for Republicans, too.

Over the past 18 months, the Fight Oligarchy tour has packed basketball
arenas, outdoor civic spaces, and theaters with tens of thousands of people,
spanning urban, rural, red, blue and purple districts. Here's a crowd shot I
took last year of the Fight Oligarchy stop in Denver, Colorado. The red arrow
points to then-recently-fired FTC Commissioner Alvaro Bedoya on stage amid a
sea of 34,000 people:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!VKLW!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbc1ba9bb-84ca-4316-a016-87bb5965c2b1_487x353.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!VKLW!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbc1ba9bb-84ca-4316-a016-87bb5965c2b1_487x353.png)

The tour is ongoing. A couple of weeks ago, Bernie made [multiple
stops](https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-
playbook/2026/09/29/a-bernie-sanders-rally-in-valadaos-backyard-01096509)
across California with Rep. Ro Khanna and CA Working Families Party Director
Jane Kim to support Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax, and he's spent the
last two weeks plowing through Florida and Texas, supporting the Senate
campaigns of Angie Nixon and James Talarico.

Here's what BIG [said](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/monopoly-round-up-
the-populist-revolt) in February 2025:

> Sanders seemed to have tapped into something. An argument about who holds
> power, a sense of broad popular rage at the perception that this country is
> now run by a small group of billionaires and corporate elites. For the first
> time since November, parts of the public are listening to political
> arguments again.
>
> And the more you zoom back, the more you see that the populist frustration
> is real, deep, and broad. [Take electric
> utilities](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/power-moves-how-electric-
> utility). On the eastern shore of Maryland, a Republican area, [twenty
> thousand people](https://www.wboc.com/news/thousands-sign-petition-
> targeting-increase-in-delmarva-power-
> bills/article_3aab31ec-e4e4-11ef-a634-cb2349ba38d8.html) have signed a
> petition demanding an investigation of Delmarva Power, a subsidiary of
> utility giant Exelon, for overcharging them. That's almost 5% of the whole
> customer base. You see the [same
> anger](https://ny1.com/nyc/manhattan/politics/2025/02/21/union-workers-
> protest-against-coned-proposed-rate-hikes) in New York City about ConEdison,
> or in St Joseph, Missouri, about
> [Evergy](https://www.newspressnow.com/news/local_news/consumer/concerned-
> residents-speak-out-on-proposed-evergy-rate-
> increase/article_9ef4d6ce-4dc4-11ef-ab43-2fd31774aeaf.html).

### "Data Center Darline"

Again, there are two questions at play here: whether populism can win
elections, which we'll know more about on Tuesday, and whether it can convert
to a governing agenda. Before I get into where I'm concerned, here's where I'm
optimistic: Bernie's Fight Oligarchy tour has largely succeeded at setting the
tone of the midterm elections, breaking out of the sandbox on the left. And
he's done so by seizing specific frustrations early on, putting forward
actionable policy, and building something that looks like a political
movement.

Let's take a specific example: data centers. In December 2025, Bernie became
the first member of Congress to
[endorse](https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/eenews/2025/12/17/bernie-
sanders-endorses-data-center-moratorium-00694062) a moratorium on data
centers. He was early to recognize that while AI was contributing to general,
abstract anxiety, data centers were a physical symbol you could point at. More
than just a symbol, they threatened to
[hike](https://ceepr.mit.edu/workingpaper/who-pays-for-growth-evidence-from-
datacenters-and-the-grid) your utility rates and
[compete](https://www.universityofcalifornia.edu/news/data-center-water-
spikes-could-billions) for allocation of water. Data centers were (and remain)
intrinsically [linked](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/how-ai-can-enable-
public-surveillance/) to a massive public surveillance operation - _they_ were
spending billions of dollars on building ugly, loud monstrosities to process
_your_ data. And the polling [flipped](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-
reads/2026/09/22/americans-views-of-data-centers-have-turned-more-negative/),
from public support among those who knew about them, to broad opposition as
more and more people started paying attention. In March 2026, Bernie and his
Fight Oligarchy tour-mate Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
[introduced](https://www.sanders.senate.gov/press-releases/news-sanders-
ocasio-cortez-announce-ai-data-center-moratorium-act/) an AI data center
moratorium in Congress.

Critically, there was something to be done about it, because states and cities
could act. By July, New York Governor Kathy Hochul, who two years earlier had
[launched](https://www.governor.ny.gov/news/governor-hochul-launches-empire-
ai-consortium-make-new-york-global-leader-artificial) an "EmpireAI" initiative
to attract AI infrastructure investment and research to her state, had signed
an Executive Order [declaring](https://www.governor.ny.gov/news/first-
statewide-moratorium-new-hyperscale-data-centers-launched-governor-kathy-
hochul) the first statewide moratorium on data center construction.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!M87E!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F05d43be9-9edd-4244-9807-fdea46a1eb75_506x336.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!M87E!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F05d43be9-9edd-4244-9807-fdea46a1eb75_506x336.jpeg)In
April 2024, Gov. Hochul launched EmpireAI to attract AI research and
investment to the state.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!aS6_!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F863572f2-211c-49fc-80c9-facac4c96d4f_476x317.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!aS6_!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F863572f2-211c-49fc-80c9-facac4c96d4f_476x317.jpeg)What
a difference two years and a popular political movement makes: In July 2026,
Gov. Hochul signed the first statewide moratorium on AI data centers.

I'm glad Governor Hochul's thinking evolved, because it's a sign that we still
live in a democracy where political outcomes are informed by public sentiment.
In just the past few years, familiarity with AI has increased across all age
groups, and so have [negative
attitudes](https://news.gallup.com/poll/712751/americans-cool-toward.aspx);
particularly among young people, where nearly half (47%) now believe AI does
more harm than good, up from 27% in 2024. Across all demographics, just 9% of
people think AI does more good than harm. There are bigger issues at hand if
our politics isn't responding to these dismal numbers.

Still, one of the larger challenges for democracy is the conflict between
majority -- or at least plurality -- sentiment and the distortive impact of
unlimited campaign spending. Bernie recognizes this more than perhaps any
other political figure of our generation, and the Fight Oligarchy tour was
more than a message; it was about building a movement with a shot at upending
the top-down orientation of politics. And that wasn't a partisan question; the
fights over money happened as much within parties as between them. In
Michigan, anti-monopolist Abdul El-Sayed
[defeated](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/boom-an-anti-monopolist-smashed-
the) corporate candidate Haley Stevens in the Democratic primary. (You can
listen to El-Sayed's
[conversation](https://www.organizedmoney.fm/p/a-conversation-with-abdul-el-
sayed) with Matt Stoller and Dave Dayen on Organized Money, if you're
interested in his views on market power.)

A record-setting _**$12 billion**_ has been
[spent](https://ncijnetwork.com/opensecrets-predicts-record-12-billion-in-
midterm-election-spending-opensecrets/) on the 2026 midterms, according to
OpenSecrets. That includes $3.9 billion in _outside_ spending, an 85% increase
over the amount spent by outside groups in the last midterm election in 2022.
A separate count by Public Citizen
[found](https://www.citizen.org/article/millionaires-and-billionaires-
fuel-2026-super-pac-spending/) that over a third of that total fundraising,
approximately $4.2 billion, is attributable to just 515 individuals. And $445
million - _**nearly 4% of every dollar spent in the 2026 election -**_**is
attributable to[one individua](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/elon-musk-
just-threatened-the-coming)**[l](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/elon-musk-
just-threatened-the-coming).

A central pillar of the Fight Oligarchy tour has been that such money in
politics [undermines](https://www.commondreams.org/news/bernie-sanders-
citizens-united) the responsiveness of candidates and elected officials to the
concerns of their constituents. Even by mid-September 2026, there were
[reports](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/17/democrats-ai-regulation-
midterms-warnings-01082564) that some Democratic consultants were advising
candidates against talking about artificial intelligence for fear of
attracting opposition spending from AI boosters. Ironically, one of the
[sources](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/01/30/ai-industry-super-pac-raises-
campaign-money.html) of that opposition spending was billionaire Democratic
mega-donor Ron Conway's Leading the Future PAC.

Ultimately, it was Conway who was cowed. By mid-October, Conway was using the
press to communicate [regret](https://www.politico.com/newsletters/decoded-by-
politico/2026/10/12/ron-conways-latest-regret-01116022) for his pro-AI
campaign. More recent [reporting](https://sfstandard.com/2026/10/31/losing-
donors-fire-ai-industry-super-pac-retreats/) shows that the pro-AI SuperPAC
Leading the Future is in retreat. And as of last week, one week out from
Election Day, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, a [$250
million](https://www.fec.gov/data/committee/C00000935/) juggernaut behind
dozens of hotly-contested races across the country, had
[settled](https://thehill.com/policy/technology/6175681-dccc-targets-gop-ai-
data-centers/) on its closing message:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!P8Ld!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff17104f3-a674-453a-97d7-862543459743_1206x1339.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!P8Ld!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff17104f3-a674-453a-97d7-862543459743_1206x1339.png)

And this messaging isn't some niche lefty thing, but is pervasive across the
board. Perhaps the greatest sign of Bernie's success is "[Data Center
Darline](https://datacenterdarline.com/)," the schoolyard taunt for Republican
Senate candidate in blood red South Carolina, Darline Graham Nordone.
According to one recent [poll](https://onpointpolitics.substack.com/p/south-
carolina-poll-andrews-leads), her Democrat opponent Annie Andrews is now
polling 3.5 points ahead of Graham Nordone among all voters and among
undecided voters, for a seat that hasn't been occupied by a Democrat in over
two decades. I don't want to speculate on outcomes, but it's clear that the
anti-data center oligarchy message resonates among all voters.

According to that same October 19 poll of South Carolina voters, Andrews is
looking to win some 11% of Trump voters in 2024. At this point, Trump seems to
be limping along, about to enter a prolonged lame duck of his term, and, like
Biden before him, is stuck with little choice but to champion an economy that
everyone hates. According to the latest Pew Research
[poll](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2026/10/08/cost-concerns-dominate-
as-publics-economic-ratings-turn-more-negative/), only 36% of Republicans see
the economy as in excellent or good shape, down from 41% in July. About a
quarter of Republicans (23%) now say conditions are poor, up from 19% in July.

And Republicans are almost perfectly split on whether Trump has had a positive
or negative effect on the economy, a huge shift from earlier this year. As of
the October 8th
[poll](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2026/10/08/economy-ranks-as-top-
issue-in-midterms-for-all-voters-but-partisans-differ-over-the-importance-of-
other-issues/) by Pew Research, 39% of Republicans say Trump's policies have
made economic conditions better -- down from 47% last fall and 57% in January
-- and 35% _of_ Republicans say Trump's policies have made things worse -- _up
from 18% at the start of the year_.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yi-t!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F154e70cc-a828-4b26-b1b6-e6ef84a63570_648x672.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yi-t!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F154e70cc-a828-4b26-b1b6-e6ef84a63570_648x672.png)

So it's no surprise that Bernie's message on data centers and Big Tech and
oligarchy is breaking the partisan molds. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis is
ditching Trump's feverish support for data center buildouts too, and Florida
Senate Candidate Angie Nixon eyes a win over Republican Ashley Moody while
campaigning for a data center moratorium.

And in South Carolina, it's no surprise that "Data Center Darline," which
serves as a proxy for the [historically low
trust](https://www.marketingcharts.com/industries/technology-239149) in the
institutions of Big Tech, is sticking, in a place that hasn't seen a toss up
election in a long time.

Data centers are far from the only election issue with Bernie's imprimatur. In
California, the Prop 40 [billionaire wealth
tax](https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-
proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) is obviously and inextricably
linked to Bernie's fight against oligarchy. On June 29, 2025, Senator Sanders
delivered a [speech](https://www.sanders.senate.gov/press-releases/prepared-
remarks-sanders-on-the-worst-bill-in-modern-u-s-history/) on the floor of the
Senate decrying Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) as "an absolute
reflection of a corrupt campaign finance system that allows billionaires to
buy elections."

In perfect parallel, California's one-time 5% tax on billionaire wealth tax is
[designed](https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-
what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/), at least rhetorically, to
back fill the loss of federal healthcare funding caused by the OBBBA. And the
near $326 million being
[spent](https://news.ballotpedia.org/2026/10/26/with-798-9-million-in-
contributions-and-counting-2026-is-the-most-expensive-ballot-measure-election-
cycle-in-california/) to oppose it -- and to support additional limits on the
state's ability to impose future taxes -- is a test of the [political purchase
power](https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/23/building-a-better-
california-321-million-prop-40-41-42-brin-schmidt-doerr/) of the state's
billionaire tech titans.

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!BGJM!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8cfdcd4e-04dc-4308-a777-d831a2c218a4_1002x350.png)

A single committee opposing Prop 40 has out-fundraised the largest labor union
in the state by a factor of 10-to-1.

The populist movement to fight oligarchy has shown up elsewhere, too. It's the
groundswell that contributed to Mayor Mamdani's
[victory](https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2025/06/25/zohran-mamdani-
win-what-does-it-mean-00424594) in New York, as Politico signaled potential
broader shifts in American politics. In Florida, Democrat candidate for Senate
Angie Nixon is [campaigning](https://angienixon.com/priorities/) not just on
the data center moratorium, but on breaking up concentrated tech monopolies,
banning surveillance pricing, and an _annual_ 5% wealth tax on the state's
billionaires. In Nebraska, Independent candidate for Senate Dan Osborn is
[running](https://www.osbornforsenate.com/plans) an explicitly populist
campaign to break up the big meatpackers, break up the Visa-Mastercard
duopoly, restrict surveillance pricing, and end the vertical integration of
health plans, PBMs and pharmacies.

There are many others - look at Hallie Shoffner's "[prairie
populism](https://prospect.org/2026/10/08/prairie-populist-crimson-red-
arkansas-hallie-shoffner/)" in deep red Arkansas, or El-Sayed's populist
healthcare-focused [campaign](https://www.levernews.com/abdul-el-sayed-isnt-
messing-around-about-healthcare/) in Michigan -- but the broader point is that
however the midterm election turns out on Tuesday, the mandate is obvious.
That's one reason the Congressional Progressive Caucus, the lefty part of
Congress, has [introduced](https://progressives.house.gov/press-
releases?ID=DD663DD7-1BCE-4683-9352-CDDE4ECAFCE6) a resolution opposing a
bailout of AI firms. It's a line in the sand for both parties.

### Are Democrats Still the Party of Nervous Lawyers?

Still, even as Bernie ran his tour, there was skepticism at the time about
whether all of that energy could hold, and whether this aspirational vision of
politics can transform frustration into action. Even if Democrats perform well
on Tuesday, which some are [predicting](https://www.theguardian.com/us-
news/ng-interactive/2026/nov/01/us-midterms-trump-blue-wave) could be more of
a flood than a wave, the more important question remains: Can they actually
transform rhetoric into governance?

Populist rhetoric, as we saw with Obama in 2008, does not necessarily mean
there will be a coherent governing agenda to prioritize the middle class. And
media and economic elites are already showing why skepticism [is
warranted](https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2026/10/24/voters-angry-
about-high-prices-may-get-little-relief-next-congress/). Here's Obama's chief
economic advisor Jason Furman, preemptively excusing inaction on the issues
that matter most to voters:

> "There is nothing the next Congress can do about the level of prices," said
> Jason Furman, a top White House economic adviser to President Barack Obama.
> "They will remain very high."

To govern, Democrats will have to ignore their economic advisors that ruined
the Biden administration framework. And I'm not sure they can.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!BE02!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffb22141a-58ca-4bed-a7c0-29a751e1e12c_813x420.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!BE02!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffb22141a-58ca-4bed-a7c0-29a751e1e12c_813x420.png)

It's true that Congress is limited in its ability to directly force the White
House's hand, but that's not Furman's argument. He simply doesn't think it's
possible to lower prices without fostering a massive recession, regardless of
political constraints. And he believes this theory even as we see
[headlines](https://www.wsj.com/health/healthcare/affordable-care-act-rates-
to-rise-steeplyagain-986da40c) in politically structured markets like health
insurance.

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!zLQi!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb663e550-0f9e-47a2-b8c4-5f3b9bb507cb_679x240.png)

So the question is whether newly elected Democrats will even _try_ to move an
agenda that points to something other than learned helplessness. And there's a
quiet internal debate over that question among Democrats in Congress: Just 10
days prior to Election Day, on October 22, Democratic Senator Brian Schatz
went on CNN to argue against an agenda that includes anything President Trump
might veto, advocating _against_ a "more aspirational" or "bold" approach:

Rep. Greg Casar, Chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus,
[responded](https://x.com/RepCasar/status/2116160217884856694) by arguing that
Democrats might win the election, but would still be seen as "the party of
nervous lawyers who just tinker around the edges" until they actually voted to
root out "rampant corruption" and deliver "higher paychecks and lower prices."
It was not enough to be anti-Trump, he argued. Democrats had to "crack down on
corporate greed to bring down the cost of health care, housing, child care,
groceries, and gas," as well as doing oversight of the White House _and_ big
business. If Trump vetoed good bills, "we'll run on them in 2028 and pass them
in 2029."

This debate is taking place among Democrats during an insurgent midterm
election cycle, but Republicans are approaching their own factional war. It's
not just DeSantis breaking from Trump's AI boosterism. In fact, most GOP
politicians have begun
[distancing](https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/08/23/most-gop-
politicians-now-talk-negatively-about-data-centers-data-shows/) themselves
from the toxicity of data centers, usually landing short of calling for a
moratorium by projecting a need for local control:

And Republican voters are increasingly defecting from the Trump administration
with frustrations aimed at Wall Street, Big Tech, and financial regulations.
According to an October 29
[poll](https://www.responsiblelending.org/sites/default/files/nodes/files/research-
publication/crl-afr-polling-memo-oct2026.pdf), 50% of Republicans think Wall
Street has too much control over the economy, and 53% think Big Tech has too
much control. Sixty percent of Republicans think the crypto industry has too
much influence in Washington, and 75% think crypto donations will "buy
dangerous policy." Eightyone percent of Republicans are concerned about
private equity takeovers. In a rebuke of Trump's dissolution of the Consumer
Financial Protection Bureau, 80% of Republicans want more stringent consumer
protections for new financial products, and 77% favor the CFPB after hearing a
description of the agency and its mission.

The question for Congress, irrespective of the midterm outcomes, is whether
either party will leverage these sentiments, which cut across traditional
political boundaries, to do something about it. Eleven of thirteen elections
this century have been "change" elections, meaning there was a change in party
control over the House, Senate or Presidency. If no one will seize the mantle,
we can expect more of the same, which is to say, more volatility, more unrest,
and bolder demands for change, wherever that change may come from. And given
the [rumbling](https://www.wsj.com/finance/stocks/ai-selloff-deepens-oil-
jumps-and-crypto-falls-4703d21b) we're starting to see in the financial
markets, there might be a lot of pressure to govern, fairly soon.
